title: Recursion in Python: Base Cases, Call Stacks, and Decomposition
content:
Recursion occurs when a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem.

Two Mandatory Rules:
1. Base Case: The condition that stops recursion. Without it, Python exceeds its stack limit (`RecursionError`).
2. Recursive Step: The function calls itself with smaller or decremented inputs moving toward the base case.

Example - Factorial:
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1: # Base case
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1) # Recursive call

Example - Fibonacci:
def fibonacci(n):
    if n <= 0: return 0
    if n == 1: return 1
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2)

Common Mistakes:
1. Missing base case or condition never reached.
2. Exceeding default call stack limit (1000 in Python).
analogy: Recursion is like Russian nesting dolls: you open each outer doll (recursive step) until you reach the solid tiny doll in the center (base case), then assemble your way back up.
simplification_tips: Always write the `if n <= 1: return ...` base case first before writing any recursive call!
